name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,884

clue.text: Italian child leaving home with nothing shoots to eat (6)

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer is a mass noun: you buy bamboo shoots by the tin but the plant itself has no plural.

indicators.note: Somebody leaving goes out, and here it is two letters of the wordplay that walk off rather than the child.

blocks.note: a bambino is an Italian baby or young child
somebody at home is in, and those are the two letters that go
nothing is written as a round zero, the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a teenager moving out with no money. Both of the crossword conventions here are worth owning: at home is IN, and nothing is O.
explanation.definitionFit: shoots to eat -> BAMBOO: the young canes of the plant are the vegetable sold for stir-fries, so the plant is named by its edible part.

clue.text: Cool, trick answer entered upside down (5)

indicators.note: A word put into the grid the wrong way up reads from its far end, so the pieces below are assembled first and then turned.

blocks.note: to trick somebody is to fool them
A is the short form of answer, the letter beside the solution in a quiz book

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface admits to being an instruction: it reads as a card trick going in the wrong way round, and the two pieces queue up in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool -> ALOOF: cool here is manner rather than temperature, the distance somebody keeps from other people, as in a cool reception.

clue.text: Make criminal steal flip-flops (3)

indicators.note: To flip-flop is to swap completely to the opposite position, so the three letters in front arrive the other way round.

blocks.note: to nab something is to steal it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is beachwear being pinched. 'Make criminal' looks like a phrase about corrupting a person, and it means outlawing an act instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Make criminal -> BAN: banning something is what turns doing it into an offence, so the verb converts a legal act into an illegal one.

clue.text: Suspect severe cop exposed witness unintentionally (7)

indicators.note: Anything suspect cannot be taken as it stands, and letters that cannot be taken as they stand are not in their proper order.
Stripped of its covering, the word keeps nothing but what was underneath the outside letters.

blocks.note: six of the seven letters, handed over to be rebuilt
take the C and the P off the outside of cop and a single letter is left

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday sense of the answer is to supervise, and that is the reading to put aside: the setter wants the older sense, seeing by accident.
explanation.definitionFit: witness unintentionally -> OVERSEE: besides supervising, to oversee is to happen to see something not meant for you, the eye's version of overhearing.

clue.text: Macabre S Korean survival show shunned by American press (7)

indicators.note: What is shunned is kept out, so the two letters named next never make it into the grid.

blocks.note: Squid Game is the Korean series in which contestants play playground games for their lives
American shortens to Am, and that pair is what gets shunned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' invites you to think of newspapers, which fits the surface about a television show and is the wrong sense entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: press -> SQUIDGE: to squidge something is to squash it between your fingers, pressing soft stuff out of shape rather than pressing a shirt.

clue.text: Cloud begins lifting around you (7)

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a piece being lifted is read from the bottom of the column towards the top.
What goes around something encloses it, so the single letter sits inside the longer piece rather than beside it.

blocks.note: to begin is to start, and this is the word before it is turned
U is the text-message spelling of you

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a weather report, where cloud lifting is exactly what you would expect it to say, so neither instruction word looks like one.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloud -> STRATUS: stratus is the low grey sheet that covers the whole sky, one of the standard cloud classes, so the general word names a particular kind.

clue.text: Disorderly house women left, lacking family values? (11)

indicators.note: A disorderly house is a brothel on the surface; taken as an instruction the word says these letters are in no proper order.

blocks.note: ten of the eleven letters, taken straight from the two words
L is left, as stamped inside a pair of boots

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disorderly house' is a set phrase, which is why it reads as one thing and works as two: the adjective is the instruction and the noun is material.
explanation.definitionFit: lacking family values -> UNWHOLESOME: something unwholesome is morally unhealthy, the word a tabloid reaches for about what children should not watch.

clue.text: Duke vacated seat taken by needy customer at bank (9)

indicators.note: A vacated building has everybody out of the middle and only its walls standing, so the word keeps its first and last letters.
If the seat has been taken by somebody, they are sitting round it, so the shorter piece goes inside the longer one.

blocks.note: the walls of the word, its middle emptied out
the needy are the poor, and these four letters open up to take the next piece
to seat somebody is to sit them down

explanation.walkthrough: A duke's seat is his country house, which is the picture the surface is painting; the wordplay wants the plain verb instead.
explanation.definitionFit: customer at bank -> DEPOSITOR: a depositor is whoever pays money into an account, so the bank's customer is named by the one thing they do there.

clue.text: Make vase out of your mug? (4)

indicators.note: A mug is slang for the face, so what comes out of yours is spoken, and the sound is what has to go in the grid.

blocks.note: the vase is an urn, most often the one that holds ashes, and it is the sound of that word you want

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has you throwing a pot out of your own drinking cup, and 'make' looks like part of that instruction rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Make -> EARN: to make a living is to earn one, the sense of make that applies to money you are paid rather than money you find.

clue.text: Yogi, say, won Barbera endless spoils (5,4)

indicators.note: Something endless never reaches its finish, so the name gives up the letter at its end.
Goods that have spoiled have gone out of shape, and letters out of shape no longer sit in the order they were given.

blocks.note: three of the nine letters, taken exactly as written
the grape's name one letter shorter, and the other six letters of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Yogi was drawn by the Hanna-Barbera studio, so the fodder and the definition come out of the same cartoon; 'say' is what marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Yogi, say -> BROWN BEAR: the Jellystone Park cartoon character is drawn as one, so 'say' flags a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Wave's concave shape beneath hulls (8)

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so the piece put beneath the other one comes lower in the column and therefore later in the word.

blocks.note: the hulls of grain are its husks, milled off as bran
a shallow curve is a dish, which is how the satellite aerial got its name

explanation.walkthrough: Waves and hulls make the surface nautical and neither word is doing nautical work: one is the definition, the other is breakfast cereal.
explanation.definitionFit: Wave -> BRANDISH: to brandish a sword is to wave it about as a threat or a display, so it is waving with menace behind it.

clue.text: Arm waving in front of driver with decapitated snake (5)

definitions.text: Arm waving in front of driver

indicators.note: A decapitated word has lost its head, so the snake arrives without its first letter.

blocks.note: w is the standard short form of with, the one used in recipes and notes
the snake is a viper, and its head has been cut off

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole picture of a windscreen fitting, described so plainly that it reads as surface, while 'with' quietly does duty as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Arm waving in front of driver -> WIPER: a windscreen wiper is a hinged arm that sweeps to and fro across the glass ahead of the driver.

clue.text: Though less than satisfactory, what EV's range is? (2,3,2,2,4)

blocks.note: the concession you make when something is true only up to a point: fine, but do not push it further
an electric vehicle's range is the distance it will cover on one charge, read here as plain measurement

explanation.walkthrough: EV is the everyday abbreviation for an electric vehicle. The first half is idiom and the second is literal, which is what makes the two readings feel so different.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves -> AS FAR AS IT GOES: the idiom grants approval only up to a limit, and an electric car's range is literally the distance it travels.

clue.text: Smallest union member wobbly on his ladder (5,6)

indicators.note: Something wobbly will not stay put in the position it was given, so the three words after it are rebuilt in another order.

blocks.note: eleven letters across three words, which is the whole of the material

explanation.walkthrough: The Union is the United States, so a union member is one of the fifty; the surface's decorator teetering on a ladder has nothing to do with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Smallest union member -> RHODE ISLAND: of the fifty American states this one covers the least ground, so 'member' means a state rather than a trade unionist.

clue.text: Helpful diner ordered in hurry (8)

indicators.note: Ordered here means put in a different order rather than tidied up, so the five letters before it are rearranged.
The rearranged letters go in: inside the piece that follows, splitting it open rather than sitting next to it.

blocks.note: to fly is to hurry, and this piece opens up to take the other letters
the five letters of diner in a new arrangement

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a restaurant evening, and 'ordered in' reads as one phrase about takeaway food rather than as two separate instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Helpful -> FRIENDLY: a friendly face is a helpful one, the word covering willingness to assist as much as actual affection.

clue.text: Settle back in bed? OK, reluctantly (7)

indicators.note: The back of a word is its final letter, and 'in' points at which word to take it from.

blocks.note: the last letter of the three, and all that is wanted
a grudging agreement is I s'pose, with suppose worn down to one syllable

explanation.walkthrough: 'Settle back in bed' reads as one comfortable phrase, and that is the trap: the definition stops after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Settle -> DISPOSE: to dispose of a matter is to settle it once and for all, the sense kept in the phrase 'the case was disposed of'.

clue.text: Bank blown up in winter? (9)

blocks.note: the surface offers a high street branch, which makes 'blown up' an explosion; a bank is also any heaped-up mass of stuff
the wind does the heaping here, piling what has fallen against a wall or a hedge until it is deep enough to close a lane

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart. The clue is one picture read twice, a robbery on the surface and a blocked country road underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue -> SNOWDRIFT: a drift is a heap piled up by the wind, so 'bank' and 'blown up' are describing one thing and not two.

clue.text: Top part of UK for cider and nice apple (7)

blocks.note: cider country is the West Country, Somerset and Devon, in the south-west corner of England
in a British greengrocer's an eater is an apple for eating raw, as against a cooker

explanation.walkthrough: 'Top part of UK' sends you to Scotland, and the cider is what tells you to look south-west instead. Nothing here announces itself as wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Top -> SWEATER: in a clothes shop a top is any upper garment, and a sweater is one of them, so the general word names it by category.

clue.text: Orpheus played for support underground, perhaps (5,2)

indicators.note: Played reads as a lyre being performed on, but to play with something is to move it about, which is what happens to the seven letters.

blocks.note: the letters of the name, all seven of them, given a different order

explanation.walkthrough: Orpheus went down to the underworld to fetch Eurydice and played his way past its guards, so every word of the surface is his story.
explanation.definitionFit: support underground, perhaps -> SHORE UP: to shore up is to prop with timbers, the job done to a mine tunnel, which is what 'perhaps' points at.

clue.text: Potentially big game that woman starts with deep breath (7)

indicators.note: If she starts with the breath then the breath is written first and she follows on behind it.

blocks.note: a pant is the breath you take when you are out of puff
her is the pronoun standing in for the woman already mentioned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Potentially big game' reads as a hopeful sports fixture, which is exactly the wrong picture: the phrase belongs to hunting, not to the fixture list.
explanation.definitionFit: Potentially big game -> PANTHER: big game is the hunter's term for large wild animals, and the big cats are the first thing on that list.

clue.text: Flog half of Scotch eggs, saving the last (7)

indicators.note: Only the front portion of the word is wanted, three letters out of its six.
To save one is to hold it back rather than spend it, so the final letter never arrives.

blocks.note: the front half of the word, three letters out of six
to egg somebody on is to urge them, and the S at the end is held back

explanation.walkthrough: A Scotch egg is one picnic item on the surface and two separate pieces of wordplay underneath, with 'eggs' as a verb rather than a food.
explanation.definitionFit: Flog -> SCOURGE: to scourge is to whip somebody, and flog is the everyday word for that punishment rather than for selling something off.

clue.text: Type that is limited by small muscles (7)

indicators.note: What limits something stands at its edges, so the outer pieces close round the middle one.

blocks.note: S is small, the letter on a clothing label
pecs are the chest muscles, short for pectorals
i.e. is the Latin id est, and it means that is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Small muscles' reads as one anatomical description and is really two pieces clued separately, which is what hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Type -> SPECIES: a species is a kind or sort, strictly the biologist's rank below genus but used loosely of any category of thing.

clue.text: Exhume Caesar's heart with Catholic priest unconcerned (13)

indicators.note: The heart of a word is what sits at its centre, here the middle pair of the emperor's six letters.

blocks.note: to disinter a body is to dig it up again
the middle two letters of the name
Father Ted, the priest in the Irish sitcom named after him

explanation.walkthrough: Father Ted is a 1990s sitcom about three Catholic priests on an island off Ireland, which is why a first name on its own can clue one.
explanation.definitionFit: unconcerned -> DISINTERESTED: strictly the word means impartial, but the sense in common use, and the one the setter wants, is simply not interested.

clue.text: Cast connected by phone to the audience (5)

indicators.note: An audience hears rather than reads, so it is the sound of the phrase that matters and not the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: a switchboard puts you through, and that word said aloud is written another way entirely

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' is a past tense here, which is what tells you the answer is one too. The trap is reading it as the people in a play, which the audience encourages.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast -> THREW: to cast a line or a stone is to throw it, and the definition sits in the past tense to match the answer.

clue.text: Unreal opportunity, those backing this magic formula claim (4)

indicators.note: The ones at the rear are meant: each word in the run gives up the letter at its back and nothing else.

blocks.note: four words, each contributing its final letter, in the order they are written

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a dodgy pitch and the people behind it, so 'those backing' reads as supporters rather than as a direction to look at the ends of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Unreal opportunity -> SCAM: the chance being offered does not exist, and the only real transaction is your money leaving.

clue.text: Source of tea in tea cups? (5)

definitions.note: The second definition names the cups rather than the ceramic they are made from, a definition by example that the question mark admits to.

blocks.note: the country the leaf first came from, and still the name printed on the caddy
the fine white ceramic they are made of, which took its name from where Europe first imported it

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are about tea and both point at the same word, which is why the clue reads as one short question rather than two definitions in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Source of tea and tea cups? both -> CHINA: tea reached Europe from that country, and the porcelain the cups are made of is named after it too.

clue.text: Hot breezes please setter in salon (9)

blocks.note: H is hot, the letter on the tap
an air is a light breeze, and the plural comes with it
pray is the old-fashioned please, as in pray tell me

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the word to distrust: in a crossword it usually means the person who wrote the clue, and here it is a thing that sets hair.
explanation.definitionFit: setter in salon -> HAIRSPRAY: hairspray is what holds a style in place, so it literally sets the hair, and a salon is where most of it is used.

clue.text: Man tapped on the shoulder is turning back to customer (3)

indicators.note: A piece that is turning comes out facing the other way, so its two letters swap places.
The back of a word is its last letter, and that single letter is all of it that crosses over.

blocks.note: the clue's own verb, taken at face value for its two letters
the last letter of the word, and nothing more of it

explanation.walkthrough: A sword laid on each shoulder is a knighthood, so the definition is the ceremony; the rest of the sentence is shop-floor politeness and pure surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Man tapped on the shoulder -> SIR: a knight is dubbed by a sword touched to his shoulders, and that is the title he answers to afterwards.

clue.text: Deadly sportsman twirling stick at amateur (7)

indicators.note: Something given a twirl comes back to you facing the other way, so the assembled pieces are read from their far end.

blocks.note: a rod is a stick, and this is the piece before the turn
the clue's own preposition, taken for its two letters
am is the short form of amateur, as in am-dram

explanation.walkthrough: 'Twirling stick' paints a majorette and 'deadly sportsman' an assassin with a racket. Neither picture is the one the clue means, and only one word is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly sportsman -> MATADOR: the matador is the bullfighter whose job is the kill, so 'deadly' is meant literally rather than as a compliment.

clue.text: Penetrating offensive reported after call for peace (6)

indicators.note: A word reported is passed on by sound, so what goes in the grid is the noise it makes and not its spelling.
What comes after goes second, so the sounded piece is written behind the hush rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: sh is the noise you make to quieten a room
offensive behaviour is rude, and once that sound follows the hush it is spelt differently

explanation.walkthrough: 'Penetrating offensive' reads as a military push, and that is the whole misdirection: the first word is the definition and the second is a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Penetrating -> SHREWD: a penetrating question is one that sees straight through things, which is exactly what a shrewd judgement does.
